meta.tagline: Elegance built on fourteen islands: water, design and fika

pills: Fika is not a break, it's a way of life

overview.title: Welcome to Stockholm
overview.intro: Stockholm is built not on the water but among it: fourteen islands, fifty-seven bridges, and a shining mirror of water at every corner. Gamla Stan's orange-and-yellow façades are medieval, Södermalm's rocky terraces young and free, the palaces stately, the metro stations underground art galleries. The city never states its elegance loudly — it says 'lagom': just the right amount. Buy a kanelbulle, sit by the water and let the city tune you to itself: Stockholm doesn't talk to those in a hurry.

local_word.definition: 'Not too little, not too much — just right': the one-word constitution of the Swedish philosophy of life. The milk in the coffee, the working day and the volume of a conversation should all be lagom. This moderation is the code to understanding the city.

rules.title: Fika is sacred — join in
rules.description: At least one coffee-and-pastry break (fika) a day is a social institution in Sweden: a coffee gulped standing up does not count. Sit in a café, order a kanelbulle, turn the phone face down — this is where you enter the city's rhythm.

rules.title: Cash is forgotten — even cards are getting old
rules.description: Sweden is the world's most cashless country: many cafés refuse cash, everything runs on card and phone. Don't hunt for kronor in your wallet — your contactless card is the city's key.

rules.title: Don't leave the archipelago unplanned
rules.description: Before Stockholm lies an archipelago of 30,000 islands: in an hour by ferry you reach island villages of red cottages. Seeing only the city is half the story — make at least one island a fixture of the programme.

quick_facts.sub: Arlanda Express 18 min · commuter train cheap

quick_facts.label: Getting around
quick_facts.sub: The SL card covers them all

quick_facts.label: Language
quick_facts.sub: English fluent as a mother tongue

tip.label: The Stockholm philosophy
tip.text: Whoever rushes through Stockholm only counts bridges: this city rewards sitting at the water's edge, the wind on an island ferry and long fikas. Shift to lagom tempo — that's when the city opens.

transport.title: Getting Around
transport.intro: SL's single-card system covers metro, bus, tram and the city ferries: travel between islands is public transport too — in this city the ferry is the metro's sibling.

items.title: Airport to the centre
items.description: The Arlanda Express flies to Central Station in 18 minutes; the pendeltåg commuter train does it in 38 at half the price. The Flygbussarna coach is the third option — a taxi only with the fixed price confirmed.

items.title: The Tunnelbana — the world's longest art gallery
items.description: More than 90 of the metro's stations were designed by artists: the blue line's cave stations (Kungsträdgården, T-Centralen, Solna) are a sightseeing route in themselves. Unlimited with the SL card.

items.title: The city ferries
items.description: The Djurgården ferry crosses from Slussen to the museum island in five minutes on the SL card: Stockholm's most beautiful 'bus line'. In summer extra routes open into the archipelago.

items.title: Island to island on foot
items.description: You walk from Gamla Stan to Södermalm and on to Djurgården across the bridges: distances are short, the views unbroken. Paths like Monteliusvägen turn a walk into a panorama tour.

items.title: Bikes and e-scooters
items.description: With broad cycle paths and waterside routes Stockholm suits the pedal: the Djurgården loop is the classic. Ice in winter, long light in summer — plan by the season.

callout.label: Metro tip
callout.text: Ride the blue line and tour three stations: T-Centralen's blue vines, Kungsträdgården's archaeological cave, Solna Centrum's crimson forest ceiling. The ticket is already in your pocket — the world's cheapest art tour.

stay.title: Where to Stay
stay.intro: In Stockholm every island is a different city: medieval Gamla Stan, elegant Östermalm, creative Södermalm, the green shore of Djurgården.

local_word.definition: The archipelago: the name of the 30,000-island labyrinth off Stockholm. The Swedish summer dream is a skärgård cottage — painted red, white-windowed, with a jetty to leap from. An hour by ferry, another universe.

items.name: Norrmalm (the centre)
items.description: The station, the shopping streets and the crossing of every line: a wide hotel range, easy reach to everything. Little character, high efficiency — the sensible base for a short visit.

items.name: Gamla Stan
items.description: The narrow orange-façaded lanes of the medieval island: the palace, the cathedral and lantern-lit evenings. Tourist-heavy by day, fairytale by night — the classic for a short romantic stay.

items.name: Södermalm
items.description: SoFo's vintage shops, third-wave coffee and rocky terrace views: young Stockholm lives here. Bars, design and waterside walks — the city's creative heart.

items.name: Östermalm
items.description: Broad boulevards, design galleries and the gourmet counters of the saluhall: the district for those after quiet refinement. Two steps over the bridge to Djurgården's green.

items.name: Kungsholmen and Vasastan
items.description: The city hall's island and calm neighbourhood life: waterside running paths, local restaurants, friendlier prices. Minutes to the centre by metro — for living like a local.

best_time.title: When to Go
best_time.intro: Stockholm lives by light: an endless day in summer, candlelight in winter. Both extremes are beautiful — as long as you know which one you're arriving into.

items.label: Spring
items.name: The Light Returns
items.subtitle: Spring · Cherry blossom, stretching evenings
items.description: Kungsträdgården's cherry trees turn into a pink tunnel in late April, the terraces open, and the city fills with the joy of leaving winter. Light-jacket-and-sunglasses season.

callout.label: April tip
callout.text: When the cherries bloom, go to Kungsträdgården in the morning: by noon the crowd becomes a photo queue. On the night of 30 April, Valborg bonfires burn on the city's hills — spring's official welcome.

items.label: Summer
items.name: The Endless Day
items.subtitle: Summer · 18 hours of light, archipelago season
items.description: The sun barely sets and the city moves outdoors: the island ferries fill, picnics spread in the parks, people leap into the sea from the rocks. With the Swedes on holiday the city is half local, half traveller.

callout.label: June tip
callout.text: On Midsummer weekend (mid-June) the city empties — shops close, but the archipelago celebrates: land in an island village amid flower crowns, herring and maypole dances and you've seen Sweden's heart.

items.label: Autumn
items.name: Golden Islands
items.subtitle: Autumn · Copper parks, museum season
items.description: Djurgården's trees turn copper, the air sharpens, and the museums and cafés begin to fill. September still suits an island trip; November is the month of transition to candlelight.

callout.label: October tip
callout.text: In October walk the Monteliusvägen path at sunset: a copper sky over Riddarfjärden, the city hall tower across the water — the city's most romantic half hour, and free.

items.label: Winter
items.name: Candlelight Season
items.subtitle: Winter · Christmas markets, Lucia, ice skating
items.description: The days are short but the city lights up indoors: star lamps in the windows, the Christmas market in Gamla Stan, the candle-lit Lucia processions on 13 December. An ice rink rises in Kungsträdgården, and fika hours stretch.

callout.label: December tip
callout.text: Find a ticket to a church concert on Lucia day, 13 December: the white-robed choir with candle crowns processing through a dark church is the most moving scene of the Swedish winter. Tickets vanish fast — move early.

eat.title: What to Eat
eat.intro: Swedish cooking is the elegance of simplicity: meatballs and lingonberry, rye and herring, cinnamon and cardamom — all in the shadow of fika culture.

local_word.definition: The coffee + pastry + conversation break: Sweden's most important social institution. Used as a verb too — 'ska vi fika?' (shall we fika?) is an invitation, and refusing it is poor form. Twice a day is normal.

items.name: Köttbullar — the real Swedish meatballs
items.description: Meatballs in cream sauce with mashed potato, lingonberry jam and pickled cucumber: taste them at a historic restaurant, not a furniture store. When the lingonberry's tartness balances the cream, you understand — this plate is serious business.
items.tag: At a historic restaurant · lingonberries required

items.name: Kanelbulle and kardemummabulle
items.description: The cinnamon and cardamom buns are fika's two pillars: 4 October is official Kanelbulle Day. At a good bakery try the cardamom one — locals secretly believe it superior.

items.name: The herring counter — sill and strömming
items.description: Pickled herring (sill) in its many forms is the smörgåsbord's heart; fried strömming is the standing classic. Taste them on rye at the Hötorget or Östermalm saluhall counters.
items.tag: At a saluhall · on rye bread

items.name: Räksmörgås — the shrimp mountain
items.description: A pile of mayonnaise-dressed shrimp on buttered bread with egg and dill: Sweden's open-sandwich masterpiece. The lunch classic of waterside cafés — eaten with knife and fork.

items.name: Prinsesstårta and semla
items.description: The green marzipan 'princess cake' runs all year; the semla — a cardamom bun filled with almond cream — is the seasonal star of January and February. Both are fika in festival dress.
items.tag: At a pastry shop · semla in winter

items.name: Craft beer and snaps culture
items.description: Södermalm's microbreweries have built a strong scene; at celebration tables the dill-and-caraway snaps glass rises with a song. Systembolaget (the state monopoly) closes early — plan ahead.
items.tag: In Söder's bars · snaps with a song

callout.label: Lunch tip
callout.text: The weekday 'dagens lunch' menus are the restaurant world's friendly door: main + salad + coffee at far below evening prices. Make lunch the big meal and leave the evening to fika and a bar — that's the Swedish order.

hidden_gems.title: Hidden Corners
hidden_gems.intro: Everyone sees the Vasa; these six are Stockholm's quiet layers.

items.name: Monteliusvägen
items.description: A 500-metre wooden-railed path along Södermalm's rocky ridge: Riddarfjärden, the city hall and Gamla Stan at your feet. At sunset the locals arrive with thermoses — do the same.

items.name: Skogskyrkogården
items.description: The UNESCO-listed 'Woodland Cemetery': minimalist chapels laid through a pine forest, and Greta Garbo's grave. A pilgrimage route for architects — where peace meets design, 20 minutes by metro.

items.rarity: The first pearl of the island necklace
items.name: Fjäderholmarna
items.description: A mini archipelago 25 minutes by ferry from the centre: craft workshops, waterside restaurants on the rocks and swimming against the city skyline. The pocket-sized rehearsal when there's no time for the big archipelago.

items.name: The Tunnelbana art tour
items.description: The blue line's cave stations — T-Centralen's vines, Solna's crimson forest, Kungsträdgården's archaeological garden: the world's longest art gallery, toured for the price of a ticket.

items.rarity: A fika paradise in a garden
items.name: Rosendals Trädgård
items.description: A greenhouse café amid orchards deep in Djurgården: fika among apple trees, sourdough from the wood oven, flower beds all around. The address of the city's most pastoral afternoon.

items.rarity: The city from a bare rock
items.name: Skinnarviksberget
items.description: The city's highest natural point: picnic blankets spread on Södermalm's bare rock, and the young gather at sunset. A short climb, a complete Stockholm view.

callout.label: Museum tip
callout.text: Enter the Vasa at the first hour (the big tour groups arrive at 10.30), then instead of busy Skansen consider the calm ABBA or Maritime museums two steps away. A Djurgården day is perfected by the museum + Rosendals fika combination.

traps.title: Tourist Traps
traps.intro: Stockholm is honest but expensive; its traps hide in price tags and a few tourist reflexes.

items.name: Jumping into a taxi at the airport
items.description: Taxi fares in Sweden are unregulated: with the wrong company the Arlanda-centre run can reach shocking figures.
items.instead: The Arlanda Express (18 min) or the pendeltåg commuter train (half price) — both land at Central Station. If a taxi is unavoidable, read the yellow price sticker on the door: the 'jämförpris' is the comparison rate.

items.name: Eating on Gamla Stan's main street
items.description: Västerlånggatan's tourist menus sell average food at high prices; two streets away the same money buys better cooking.
items.instead: Turn into the side lanes or cross the bridge and eat in Södermalm. In Gamla Stan do only fika — the atmosphere is free, and a bun costs the same everywhere.

items.name: Stocking up on alcohol at the restaurant
items.description: Restaurant drink prices are steep, and the supermarket shelf holds only light beer; whoever doesn't plan the evening leaves the budget at the bar.
items.instead: Do your shopping at Systembolaget (the state monopoly) in daylight — it closes early on Saturday and is shut on Sunday. In bars, follow the boards that say happy hour and 'dagens öl'.

items.name: Buying the Stockholm Pass without the maths
items.description: The city card only pays off for someone doing three paid sights a day; on a walking-and-park programme it goes to waste.
items.instead: Write your museum list, add up the entries, then decide. Remember: many state museums' permanent collections are already free — check that list first.

callout.label: Golden rule
callout.text: Most of Stockholm's finest things are free: Monteliusvägen, the metro art, the free museums, the sunsets from the rocks. Save the money for one good dinner and the archipelago ferry — the rest resolves on a lagom budget.

itinerary.title: Ready-Made Routes
itinerary.intro: If you hate planning, follow these flows. The times are flexible; keep the spirit, break the order.

plans.title: If You Have 1 Day
plans.subtitle: From the Middle Ages to an island, from the island to sunset

steps.title: Gamla Stan, empty
steps.description: The orange-façaded lanes, Stortorget square and the cathedral in morning silence: before the tour groups arrive, the medieval island is yours. Coffee on the square.

steps.title: The palace and the changing of the guard
steps.description: The changing of the guard in the Royal Palace courtyard towards noon; before it, a short dive into one of the palace museums.

steps.title: Ferry to Djurgården + the Vasa
steps.description: The five-minute ferry from Slussen to the museum island: come face to face with the Vasa, the warship that sank in 1628 and rose 333 years later — Scandinavia's most striking museum.

steps.title: Fika at Rosendals
steps.description: Kanelbulle + coffee at Djurgården's garden café: the official fika break among apple trees. Walk back along the water.

steps.title: Södermalm and Monteliusvägen
steps.description: Browse SoFo's windows, then sunset on the Monteliusvägen path: the city hall tower and Riddarfjärden in golden light.

steps.title: A Söder evening
steps.description: Köttbullar or modern Swedish cooking, then a microbrewery to close: a Stockholm night starts calm and ends warm.

plans.title: If You Have 3 Days
plans.subtitle: City, museums and archipelago — the full dose

steps.title: Classic Stockholm
steps.description: The one-day flow above: Gamla Stan, the palace, the Vasa, Rosendals, Monteliusvägen.

steps.title: Art and neighbourhoods
steps.description: The blue-line metro art tour + the City Hall in the morning; the herring counter at the Östermalm saluhall at noon; Fotografiska or ABBA in the afternoon; an evening walk on Kungsholmen's waterside + a neighbourhood restaurant.

steps.title: Archipelago day
steps.description: Morning ferry to Vaxholm or Fjäderholmarna: red cottages, swimming off the rocks, lunch at an island restaurant; stop at Skogskyrkogården on the way back (by metro); a farewell evening in lantern-lit Gamla Stan.

phrases.title: 5-Word Survival Kit
phrases.intro: Swedish is soft and melodic; everyone speaks English, but these five open doors with a smile.

items.meaning: Hello — 'hej hej' works for goodbye too
Thank you — 'tack så mycket' is thanks a lot; the word you'll hear most in Sweden
Here you go / you're welcome — the plate lands on the table with it
Cheers! — eye contact as the glass rises is the Swedish way
The coffee + bun break — if you hear 'ska vi fika?' the answer is always yes

checklist.title: Stockholm Checklist
checklist.completion_message: Tack så mycket! You've lived Stockholm in a lagom dose!
